systemsMapSummary: Under-reporting is held in place by three reinforcing loops. First, a friction loop: the only way to report is a 15-minute paper form kept by the office, not at the machine, so a near-miss on the line rarely survives the walk and the wait. Second, a black-hole loop: supervisors are slammed and rarely follow up, so operators who did report 'never heard back' and stop bothering. Third, a fear loop: the shift bonus rewards a 'zero-incident' record, so logging a near-miss feels like it dents the team's payout, and the safest move is to stay quiet. These compound — hard to report, plus nothing changes when you do, plus a reason not to, equals four reports a month. The highest-leverage moment is at the machine, right after a near-miss, when a report must be fast, obviously worth it, and safe.

topLeveragePoints.point: Put a fast, tear-off report card at every machine
topLeveragePoints.currentState: The only channel is a 15-minute paper form by the office; an operator already suggested a tear-off card at the line.

topLeveragePoints.point: Close the loop visibly — acknowledge every report and show what changed
topLeveragePoints.currentState: 'Last time I reported something, I never heard back'; supervisors rarely follow up, so reporting feels pointless.

topLeveragePoints.point: Separate near-miss reporting from the shift bonus so it can't cost the team
topLeveragePoints.currentState: The bonus's 'zero-incident' component makes operators fear a report dents the shift's payout.

headline: If reporting took two minutes at the machine, every report visibly led to action, and it couldn't dent the bonus, we'd likely see near-miss reports rise from ~4 toward a healthy leading-indicator rate — a sign risk is surfacing earlier, not that the plant got less safe.
